title: Chapter 33. Of the Number, Antiquity, Scope, Authority, and Interpreters of the Books of Holy Scripture
section: Part III — Of a Christian Commonwealth
paragraphs: By the books of Holy SCRIPTURE are meant those that ought to be the canon — that is, the rules — of Christian life. And because all the rules of life that men are in conscience bound to observe are laws, the question of Scripture is the question of what is law throughout all Christendom, both natural and civil. For though Scripture does not determine what laws each Christian king shall constitute in his own dominions, it does determine what laws he shall not constitute. Since therefore I have already proved that sovereigns in their own dominions are the sole legislators, only those books are canonical — that is, law — in every nation which are established as such by the sovereign authority. It is true that God is the sovereign of all sovereigns, and so, when he speaks to any subject, he ought to be obeyed, whatever any earthly potentate commands to the contrary. But the question is not of obedience to God, but of when, and what, God has said. To subjects who have no supernatural revelation, this can be known only by that natural reason which guided them, for the obtaining of peace and justice, to obey the authority of their several commonwealths — that is, of their lawful sovereigns. According to this obligation, I can acknowledge no other books of the Old Testament to be Holy Scripture except those that have been commanded to be acknowledged as such by the authority of the Church of England. What books these are is well enough known without setting them all out here; and they are the same as those acknowledged by St Jerome — who holds the rest (namely, the Wisdom of Solomon, Ecclesiasticus, Judith, Tobias, the first and second of Maccabees — though he had seen the first in Hebrew — and the third and fourth of Esdras) for Apocrypha. Of the canonical, Josephus, a learned Jew who wrote in the time of the Emperor Domitian, reckons twenty-two, making the number agree with the Hebrew alphabet. St Jerome does the same, though they reckon them differently. For Josephus numbers five books of Moses, thirteen of prophets who wrote the history of their own times (how that agrees with the prophetic writings contained in the Bible we shall see hereafter), and four of hymns and moral precepts. But St Jerome reckons five books of Moses, eight of prophets, and nine of other holy writings, which he calls Hagiographa. The Septuagint — seventy learned Jewish men sent for by Ptolemy, king of Egypt, to translate the Jewish law from Hebrew into Greek — have left us no other books for Holy Scripture in the Greek tongue than the same ones that are received in the Church of England.
As for the books of the New Testament, they are equally acknowledged as canon by all Christian churches, and by all sects of Christians that admit any books at all as canonical.

Who the original writers of the various books of Holy Scripture were has not been made evident by any sufficient testimony from any other history (which is the only proof of matter of fact), nor can it be by any arguments of natural reason — for reason serves only to convince of the truth, not of fact, but of consequence. The light, therefore, that must guide us in this question must be what is held out to us by the books themselves. And this light, though it does not show us the writer of every book, is yet not useless in giving us knowledge of the time when they were written.

And first, for the Pentateuch, it is not argument enough that they were written by Moses just because they are called the five books of Moses — no more than the titles 'The Book of Joshua,' 'The Book of Judges,' 'The Book of Ruth,' and 'The Books of the Kings' are arguments enough to prove that they were written by Joshua, by the Judges, by Ruth, and by the Kings. In titles of books, the subject is marked as often as the writer. 'The History of Livy' denotes the writer; but 'The History of Scanderbeg' is named from the subject. We read in the last chapter of Deuteronomy (verse 6), concerning the sepulchre of Moses, that 'no man knows of his sepulchre to this day' — that is, to the day on which those words were written. It is therefore plain that those words were written after his burial. For it would be a strange interpretation to say that Moses spoke of his own sepulchre (even by prophecy), saying that it was not to be found to that day on which he was yet living. But it may perhaps be alleged that only the last chapter, not the whole Pentateuch, was written by some other man. Let us therefore consider what we find in the book of Genesis, chapter 12, verse 6: 'And Abraham passed through the land, to the place of Shechem, to the plain of Moreh, and the Canaanite was then in the land.' These must be the words of someone writing when the Canaanite was no longer in the land — and consequently not of Moses, who died before he came into it. Likewise in Numbers 21:14, the writer cites another, more ancient, book entitled The Book of the Wars of the Lord, in which were recorded the acts of Moses at the Red Sea and at the brook Arnon. So it is sufficiently plain that the five books of Moses were written after his time, though how long after is not so plain.

But though Moses did not compile those books entirely, and in the form we have them, he wrote everything he is there said to have written: for example, the volume of the law, which is contained, as it seems, in Deuteronomy 11 and the following chapters to chapter 27 — which was also commanded to be written on stones on their entry into the land of Canaan (Deut. 31:9). And this Moses himself wrote, and delivered to the priests and elders of Israel, to be read every seventh year to all Israel at their assembling for the feast of Tabernacles. And this is the law which God commanded that their kings (once they had established that form of government) should take a copy of from the priests and Levites, to lay in the side of the ark (Deut. 31:26); and the same which, having been lost, was long afterward found again by Hilkiah and sent to King Josiah, who, causing it to be read to the people, renewed the covenant between God and them (2 Kings 22:8 and 23:1–3).

That the book of Joshua was also written long after the time of Joshua may be gathered from many places in the book itself. Joshua had set up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan as a monument to their crossing (Josh. 4:9); of which the writer says, 'They are there to this day.' For 'to this day' is a phrase that signifies a time past, beyond the memory of man. In the same way, upon the saying of the Lord that he had rolled off from the people the reproach of Egypt, the writer says, 'The place is called Gilgal to this day' (Josh. 5:9) — which would have been improper to say in the time of Joshua. So too of the name of the Valley of Achor, from the trouble Achan raised in the camp, the writer says it 'remains to this day' (Josh. 7:26) — which must therefore have been long after the time of Joshua. There are many other arguments of this kind, as Josh. 8:29; 13:13; 14:14; 15:63.

The same is plain by like arguments for the book of Judges (1:21, 26; 6:24; 10:4; 15:19; 17:6) and for Ruth (1:1), but especially Judges 18:30, where it is said that Jonathan 'and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan, until the day of the captivity of the land.'

That the books of Samuel were also written after his own time, there are the like arguments: 1 Sam. 5:5; 7:13, 15; 27:6; and 30:25 — where, after David had adjudged an equal share of the spoils to those who guarded the baggage as to those who fought, the writer says, 'He made it a statute and an ordinance to Israel to this day.' Again, when David (displeased that the Lord had slain Uzzah for putting out his hand to steady the ark) called the place Perez-Uzzah, the writer says it is called so 'to this day' (2 Sam. 6:4). The time of the writing of that book must therefore be long after the time of the fact — that is, long after the time of David.

As for the two books of the Kings and the two books of the Chronicles, beyond the passages that mention such monuments as the writer says remained to his own day — such as 1 Kings 9:13; 9:21; 10:12; 12:19; 2 Kings 2:22; 8:22; 10:27; 14:7; 16:6; 17:23; 17:34; 17:41; 1 Chron. 4:41; 5:26 — it is sufficient argument that they were written after the captivity in Babylon that their history is continued to that time. For the facts recorded are always more ancient than such books as mention and quote the register; as these books do in various places, referring the reader to the chronicles of the kings of Judah, to the chronicles of the kings of Israel, to the books of the prophet Samuel or the prophet Nathan, of the prophet Ahijah, to the vision of Iddo, to the books of the prophet Shemaiah and of the prophet Iddo.

The books of Ezra and Nehemiah were certainly written after their return from captivity, because their return, the rebuilding of the walls and houses of Jerusalem, the renewal of the covenant, and the ordination of their polity are all contained in them.
The history of Queen Esther is from the time of the captivity, and so the writer must have been of the same time, or after it.

The book of Job has no mark in it of the time when it was written. And though it sufficiently appears (from Ezekiel 14:14 and James 5:11) that he was no fictitious person, the book itself does not seem to be a history but a treatise on a question much disputed in ancient times — namely, 'why wicked men have often prospered in this world, and good men have been afflicted.' This is the most likely reading because, from the beginning to the third verse of the third chapter (where Job's complaint begins), the Hebrew is (as St Jerome testifies) in prose; and from there to the sixth verse of the last chapter, in hexameter verses; and the rest of that chapter again in prose. So the dispute is all in verse, and the prose is added only as a preface at the beginning and an epilogue at the end. But verse is not the usual style of men who are themselves in great pain, like Job, or of those who come to comfort them, like his friends — yet in philosophy, especially moral philosophy, it was frequent in ancient times.

The Psalms were written for the most part by David, for the use of the choir. To these are added some songs of Moses and other holy men, and some written after the return from the captivity, such as Psalms 137 and 126; whereby it is plain that the Psalter was compiled and put into the form it now has after the return of the Jews from Babylon.

The Proverbs, being a collection of wise and godly sayings — partly of Solomon, partly of Agur the son of Jakeh, and partly of the mother of King Lemuel — cannot probably be thought to have been collected by Solomon rather than by Agur or the mother of Lemuel; and that, though the sentences are theirs, the collecting or compiling of them into this one book was the work of some other godly man who lived after them all.

The books of Ecclesiastes and the Canticles have nothing that was not Solomon's, except perhaps the titles or inscriptions. For 'The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem,' and 'The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's,' seem to have been made for the sake of distinction at the time when the books of Scripture were gathered into one body of the law, so that not only the doctrine but also the authors might be on record.

Of the prophets, the most ancient are Zephaniah, Jonah, Amos, Hosea, Isaiah, and Micah, who lived in the time of Amaziah and Azariah (otherwise Uzziah), kings of Judah. But the book of Jonah is not properly a record of his prophecy (for that is contained in these few words: 'Forty days, and Nineveh shall be destroyed'), but a history or narrative of his perverseness in disputing God's commandments; so there is little probability he should be the author, given that he is the subject. But the book of Amos is his prophecy.
Jeremiah, Obadiah, Nahum, and Habakkuk prophesied in the time of Josiah.
Ezekiel, Daniel, Haggai, and Zechariah prophesied in the captivity.

When Joel and Malachi prophesied is not evident from their writings. But considering the inscriptions, or titles, of their books, it is plain enough that the whole Scripture of the Old Testament was set forth in the form we have it after the return of the Jews from their captivity in Babylon, and before the time of Ptolemy Philadelphus, who had it translated into Greek by seventy men sent to him out of Judea for that purpose. And if the books of Apocrypha (which the Church recommends to us, though not as canonical, yet as profitable books for our instruction) may on this point be credited, the Scripture was set forth in the form we have by Ezra; as may appear from what he himself says in 2 Esdras 14:21–22 (etc.), where, speaking to God, he says, 'Your law is burnt; therefore no man knows the things you have done, or the works that are to begin. But if I have found grace before you, send down the holy Spirit into me, and I shall write all that has been done in the world since the beginning, which were written in your law, that men may find your path, and that those who shall live in the latter days may live.' And verse 45: 'And it came to pass, when the forty days were fulfilled, that the Highest spoke, saying, "The first that you have written, publish openly, that the worthy and unworthy may read it; but keep the seventy last, that you may deliver them only to such as are wise among the people."' And this much concerning the time of the writing of the books of the Old Testament.

The writers of the New Testament all lived less than an age after Christ's ascension, and had all seen our Saviour, or been his disciples, except St Paul and St Luke; and consequently whatever was written by them is as ancient as the time of the apostles. But the time at which the books of the New Testament were received and acknowledged by the Church as their writing is not altogether so ancient. For as the books of the Old Testament come to us from no higher time than that of Ezra, who by the direction of God's Spirit retrieved them when they were lost, so the books of the New Testament — copies of which were not many, nor could easily be all in any one private man's hand — cannot be derived from a higher time than that at which the governors of the Church collected, approved, and recommended them to us as the writings of those apostles and disciples under whose names they go. The first enumeration of all the books, both of the Old and New Testament, is in the Canons of the Apostles, supposed to have been collected by Clement, the first (after St Peter) bishop of Rome. But because that is only supposed, and by many questioned, the Council of Laodicea is the first we know of that recommended the Bible to the then-Christian churches as the writings of the prophets and apostles; and this council was held in the 364th year after Christ. At which time, though ambition had so far prevailed on the great doctors of the Church that they no longer esteemed emperors (even Christian ones) as the shepherds of the people, but as sheep; and emperors who were not Christian as wolves; and they endeavoured to pass their doctrine, not as counsel and information from preachers, but as laws from absolute governors; and thought such frauds as tended to make the people the more obedient to Christian doctrine to be pious — yet I am persuaded they did not on that account falsify the Scriptures, even though the copies of the books of the New Testament were in the hands only of the ecclesiastics. For if they had had any such intention, they would surely have made them more favourable to their power over Christian princes, and to civil sovereignty, than they are. I see therefore no reason to doubt that the Old and New Testaments, as we have them now, are the true records of what was done and said by the prophets and apostles. And so perhaps are some of those books which are called Apocrypha, if left out of the canon not for any disagreement of doctrine with the rest, but only because they are not found in the Hebrew. For after the conquest of Asia by Alexander the Great, there were few learned Jews who were not perfect in the Greek tongue. The seventy interpreters who turned the Bible into Greek were all of them Hebrews; and we have extant the works of Philo and Josephus, both Jews, written by them eloquently in Greek. But it is not the writer, but the authority of the Church, that makes a book canonical.

And although these books were written by various men, it is plain that the writers were all endowed with one and the same Spirit, in that they conspire to one and the same end — the setting forth of the rights of the kingdom of God: the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. For the book of Genesis derives the genealogy of God's people from the creation of the world to the going down into Egypt; the other four books of Moses contain the election of God for their king, and the laws he prescribed for their government; the books of Joshua, Judges, Ruth, and Samuel, to the time of Saul, describe the acts of God's people until the time when they cast off God's yoke and called for a king after the manner of their neighbouring nations. The rest of the history of the Old Testament traces the succession of the line of David to the captivity, from which line was to spring the restorer of the kingdom of God — our blessed Saviour, God the Son — whose coming was foretold in the books of the prophets, after whom the evangelists wrote his life, and his actions, and his claim to the kingdom, while he lived on earth. And lastly, the Acts and Epistles of the apostles declare the coming of God the Holy Ghost, and the authority he left with the apostles and their successors for the direction of the Jews and the inviting of the Gentiles. In short, the histories and prophecies of the Old Testament, and the Gospels and Epistles of the New, have all had one and the same scope — to convert men to the obedience of God: first in Moses and the priests; second in the man Christ; and third in the apostles and the successors to apostolic power. For these three at various times represented the person of God: Moses, and his successors the high priests and kings of Judah, in the Old Testament; Christ himself in the time he lived on earth; and the apostles, and their successors, from the day of Pentecost (when the Holy Ghost descended on them) to this day.
The question of the authority of the Scriptures stated.

It is a question much disputed between the various sects of the Christian religion: from where do the Scriptures derive their authority? — which question is also sometimes propounded in other terms, as 'How do we know them to be the word of God?' or 'Why do we believe them to be so?' The difficulty of resolving it arises chiefly from the impropriety of the words in which the question itself is framed. For it is believed on all hands that the first and original author of them is God; so the question disputed is not that. Again, it is plain that none can know they are God's word (though all true Christians believe it) but those to whom God himself has revealed it supernaturally; and so the question is not rightly put as one of our knowledge of it. Lastly, when the question is put in terms of our belief — since some are moved to believe for one reason, and others for another — there can be no one general answer for them all. The question, truly stated, is: by what authority are they made law?

So far as they do not differ from the laws of nature, there is no doubt that they are the law of God, and carry their authority with them, legible to all men who have the use of natural reason; but this is no other authority than that of all other moral doctrine consonant with reason, whose dictates are laws not made, but eternal.

If they are made law by God himself, they are of the nature of written law, which are laws only to those to whom God has so sufficiently published them that no man can excuse himself by saying that he did not know they were his.

He, therefore, to whom God has not supernaturally revealed that they are his — nor that those who published them were sent by him — is not obliged to obey them, by any authority other than his whose commands already have the force of laws; that is, by any other authority than that of the commonwealth, residing in the sovereign, who alone has the legislative power. Again, if it is not the legislative authority of the commonwealth that gives them the force of laws, it must be some other authority derived from God, either private or public. If private, it obliges only the man to whom in particular God has been pleased to reveal it. For if every man were obliged to take for God's law whatever particular men, on the pretext of private inspiration or revelation, should thrust upon him (given how many men, out of pride and ignorance, take their own dreams, extravagant fancies, and madness for testimonies of God's Spirit; or out of ambition, claim such divine testimonies falsely, against their own consciences), it would be impossible that any divine law should be acknowledged. If public, it is the authority of the commonwealth or of the Church. But the Church, if it is one person, is the same thing as a commonwealth of Christians — called a commonwealth, because it consists of men united in one person, their sovereign; and a Church, because it consists of Christian men united in one Christian sovereign. But if the Church is not one person, then it has no authority at all; it can neither command nor do any action; nor is it capable of having any power or right to anything; nor has it any will, reason, or voice — for all these qualities are personal. Now if the whole number of Christians is not contained in one commonwealth, they are not one person; nor is there a universal Church that has any authority over them; and therefore the Scriptures are not made laws by the universal Church. Or, if it is one commonwealth, then all Christian monarchs and states are private persons, and subject to being judged, deposed, and punished by a universal sovereign of all Christendom. So the question of the authority of the Scriptures is reduced to this: 'Whether Christian kings, and the sovereign assemblies in Christian commonwealths, are absolute in their own territories, immediately under God; or subject to one vicar of Christ, set over the universal Church, to be judged, condemned, deposed, and put to death, as he shall think expedient or necessary for the common good.'

This question cannot be resolved without a more particular consideration of the kingdom of God; from which also we are to judge of the authority of interpreting the Scripture. For whoever has lawful power over any writing to make it law has the power also to approve, or disapprove, the interpretation of the same.
